_about: Every visitor-facing string of the Exposure Clock, checked by the style gate. Variables in braces. Every date the clock shows is a target unless a binding instrument sets it, and no string here gives a date the force of law. The question, lede and method note are drafts until Swann has reviewed them.

copy.title: Exposure Clock
copy.question: How long must your data stay secret?
copy.lede: Your data’s shelf life and migration time, set against expert estimates of quantum risk.
copy.promise: How long must your data stay secret, and will today’s encryption last that long?
copy.intro: The Exposure Clock compares how long your data must stay secret and how long your migration will take with expert estimates of when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer might exist.

copy.method: The Exposure Clock sets three quantities side by side. The first is how long your data must stay secret, and you set it. The second is how long your move to quantum-safe cryptography will take, and you set that too. The third is when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer might exist, and the Atlas does not estimate it: the band shows the ranges the experts surveyed for the {surveyTitle} give, for a machine as the survey defines it. {definition} Between surveyed horizons the band is joined by straight lines, drawn dashed because they are interpolation, never survey figures. Choosing what you protect starts the first slider from a period an institutional source documents for that kind of data: the place’s own where the Atlas holds one, otherwise an EU rule or a general one. The tool names the source and says whether the period is one of secrecy, of closed access or only of keeping, and says so plainly when the Atlas holds none. Signatures and certificates are left out: the risk measured here is to secrecy, and a forged signature is a different problem.
